content: 1. In 2017, Wijting et al. conducted a phase 2 randomized non-inferiority trial (DOMONO) to evaluate the efficacy of dolutegravir as a maintenance monotherapy for HIV. The results were published in The Lancet HIV. 2. Blanco et al. presented findings on resistance pathways in individuals failing dolutegravir monotherapy at the 2017 Conference on Retroviruses and Opportunistic Infections in Seattle, USA. 3. The World Health Organization (WHO) released guidelines in December 2014 as a supplement to the 2013 consolidated antiretroviral (ARV) guidelines. These guidelines addressed post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) for HIV and the use of co-trimoxazole prophylaxis for HIV-related infections in adults, adolescents, and children. 4. Ford et al. conducted a systematic analysis in 2015 to determine the optimal choice of antiretroviral drugs for post-exposure prophylaxis in adults and adolescents. Their findings were published in Clinical Infectious Diseases. 5. Penazzato et al. performed a systematic review in 2015 to evaluate the choice of antiretroviral drugs for post-exposure prophylaxis in children. The results were also published in Clinical Infectious Diseases. 6. WHO clinical guidelines provide recommendations for responding to children and adolescents who have been sexually abused. These guidelines are accessible on the WHO reproductive health website. 7. Wiboonchutikul et al. reported significant intolerance to efavirenz in HIV occupational post-exposure prophylaxis in a study published in The Journal of Hospital Infection in 2016. 8. WHO developed an implementation tool for pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) of HIV infection, which is available on the WHO HIV website. 9. WHO also issued guidelines on when to start antiretroviral therapy and the use of pre-exposure prophylaxis for HIV. These guidelines are accessible online. 10. Mazanderani et al. published a brief report in 2018 on declining baseline viremia and increasing discordant HIV-1 confirmatory results within South Africa's early infant diagnosis program from 2010 to 2016 in The Journal of Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndromes. 11. Feucht et al. highlighted the implications of false-positive HIV DNA PCR testing in infants in a 2012 study published in the South African Medical Journal. 12. The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services provides guidelines for the use of antiretroviral agents in pediatric HIV infection, which include recommendations for diagnosing HIV in infants and children. 13. Mazanderani et al. provided recommendations for managing indeterminate HIV PCR results within South Africa's early infant diagnosis program in a 2016 publication in the South African Journal of HIV Medicine. 14. Luzuriaga and Mofenson discussed challenges in eliminating pediatric HIV-1 infection in a 2016 article in the New England Journal of Medicine. 15. Wagner et al. reported in 2017 that rapid serology tests fail to reliably assess HIV exposure among sick hospitalized infants in a study published in AIDS. 16. Urick et al. demonstrated in 2018 that rapid serological tests are ineffective in screening for HIV exposure in HIV-positive infants. Their findings were published in The Journal of Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndromes. 17. WHO updated its recommendations on first-line and second-line antiretroviral regimens, post-exposure prophylaxis, and early infant diagnosis of HIV. These updates are detailed in annexes that include methods for developing the guidelines, drug toxicity, dosages, and diagnostic algorithms. 18. The WHO Guideline Steering Group used the GRADE methodology to assess the certainty of evidence and determine the strength of recommendations. This approach evaluates the balance between desirable and undesirable effects, resource implications, and feasibility. 19. A systematic review was conducted to assess the risk of neural tube defects associated with dolutegravir (DTG) use during the periconception period. Data from a study in Botswana and other surveillance systems were analyzed to identify potential cases. 20. Online surveys were conducted among people living with HIV, healthcare workers, and program managers to assess values, preferences, feasibility, and acceptability of the recommendations. These surveys were carried out before concerns about neural tube defects with DTG use emerged. 21. The WHO Guideline Development Group met in Geneva in May 2018 to review evidence and formulate recommendations. A follow-up meeting was held in June 2018 to confirm the recommendations in light of new safety concerns regarding DTG. 22. A draft of the guidelines was peer-reviewed by the Guideline Development Group and the External Review Group. Conflicts of interest were managed, and all comments were incorporated into the final document. 23. WHO ensured transparency by publishing declarations of interest and biographies of all contributors to the guidelines. Conflicts of interest were reviewed and managed to minimize bias in the recommendations.
